title: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
description: The Moon really does rotate. Discover the neat timing behind its familiar face—and why the far side is not always dark.

sections.title: A familiar face with a hidden turn
sections.html:
We see roughly the same side of the Moon because it turns once on its axis in the time it takes to orbit Earth once. This matching rhythm is called synchronous rotation; the Moon is tidally locked to Earth. NASA explains its orbit and rotation.

Watch the Moon on different nights and the outline changes, but its familiar dark patches keep returning. It is tempting to think the Moon never spins. In fact, a spin is what keeps that familiar face pointing towards us.

sections.title: Imagine walking around a chair
sections.html:
Picture a chair in the middle of a room. You walk around it, always keeping your face towards the chair. Halfway around, you face the opposite wall from the one you faced at the start.

By the time you complete the circle, your body has turned once. One journey around the chair, one turn of your body. That is the basic idea behind the Moon’s matching movements.

If you kept facing the same wall throughout the walk, different sides of you would face the chair. “No rotation” would not keep the same face pointing inwards.

sections.title: The far side gets sunshine too
sections.html:
Far side describes the side facing away from Earth. It does not mean a place in permanent darkness. As NASA points out, different parts of the Moon move between sunlight and darkness.

The phases of the Moon tell us how much of its sunlit half we can see. They are a change in illumination and viewpoint, not a different face swinging round for each night’s appearance.

sections.title: Why say roughly the same side?
sections.html:
Our view shifts a little over time. The Moon appears to nod and rock, letting us glimpse slightly around its edges. This effect is called libration, and NASA’s Moon phases page explains it.

So “the same side” is a useful starting point, rather than a perfectly frozen view. The important distinction stays simple: the Moon rotates, and its rotation matches its orbit. Next time those dark patches look familiar, there is a turn hiding behind that familiar face.

questions.prompt: Why does roughly the same side of the Moon face Earth?
options: It rotates once for each orbit of Earth
questions.explanation: The Moon makes one turn on its axis in the time it takes to orbit Earth once. This is synchronous rotation.

questions.prompt: What does the far side of the Moon mean?
options: The side that never gets sunlight
The side facing away from Earth
The side that is always full
questions.explanation: Far side names its direction relative to Earth. It has periods of sunlight and darkness too.

options: The Moon’s apparent rocking that reveals a little more around its edges
questions.explanation: Libration slightly changes our view of the Moon, allowing glimpses around its edges over time.
